title: The Transfiguration (6 August)
hook: the mountain of light, on the same date as Hiroshima's bombing

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary Magdalene, sent from an empty tomb with news. Your line was she told them first. Whose witness did you honor? Day one thousand forty-seven.

Three fishermen are climbing behind their teacher, up a high mountain, apart from everyone. Peter, James and John. Somewhere near the top, the man they have been following changes in front of them. His face shines like the sun. His clothes go white as light. Two figures from the old stories are standing there talking with him. And Peter, who Mark says did not know what to say, offers to build some shelters. The church remembers that mountain on the date in today's title, the sixth of August. In a later century, that same date became the day an atomic bomb fell on the city of Hiroshima. One date, two lights. Today, The Transfiguration.

Matthew, Mark and Luke all tell this story. Here is Matthew, in the King James Bible: Jesus "was transfigured before them: and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light." Transfigured means his form changed. Not a costume, not a trick of the sunset. Then Moses and Elijah appear, the King James spells it Elias, talking with him. Some readers hear the law and the prophets in those two figures, standing beside Jesus. Peter blurts out: "Lord, it is good for us to be here: if thou wilt, let us make here three tabernacles; one for thee, and one for Moses, and one for Elias." He wants to keep the moment, to pitch a tent around it. Before he finishes, a bright cloud covers them, and a voice says: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him." The disciples fall on their faces, terrified. And then a quiet moment. Jesus comes and touches them, and says, "Arise, and be not afraid." They look up, and Matthew says they "saw no man, save Jesus only." Then they walk back down the mountain, into ordinary need. Orthodox churches keep this feast, and Catholic and some Protestant calendars keep it too. And the date carries a second light now. On the day the church reads about a light that ends with, be not afraid, a light that burns was loosed on a city and made a whole city afraid. Some churches mark both together, with prayer for peace. The story doesn't make that second light smaller. It just stands beside it.
screen: `HIS FACE DID SHINE AS THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for peace, or hold it in mind. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one place where people are afraid tonight because of war. Don't search for the worst image. Just name the place. Then bring to mind Jesus touching his friends on the mountain, and the words, arise, and be not afraid. If you pray, you can offer Jesus's own words from the Sermon on the Mount: blessed are the peacemakers. If you don't, just hold that place, and the people in it, quietly, for the length of the sit. The bell holds the time.
The Transfiguration. The moment on the mountain when Jesus's face shone like the sun, and a voice said, hear ye him. Kept on the sixth of August, the same date as the bombing of Hiroshima.
Your line: two lights. Today, when you switch on a light, let it remind you of the mountain, and of one place that needs peace. Day one thousand forty-seven.

howItsDone: Orthodox, Catholic and some Protestant churches keep the Transfiguration on the sixth of August with readings of the mountain story, and some churches join it with prayers for peace because it shares the date of the Hiroshima bombing.

original.note: Greek, Matthew 17:2: he was transfigured, his form was changed.

trapdoor: what you thought: a mysterious glow on a mountain long ago.
what it means: three friends see Jesus shining, hear a voice say hear ye him, and are told, arise, and be not afraid.
what a scholar hears: Luke adds that Moses and Elias spoke of his decease at Jerusalem; the Greek word there is exodos.

notes: Claims rule: the sixth of August comes from the index title; the Hiroshima date is from the index hook and is not in the cited text. Confirm the feast date and the framing are acceptable; no year or casualty figures are given.
'Catholic and some Protestant calendars keep it too' and 'Orthodox Christians treasure this feast' are general claims; soften if a Keeper prefers.
'Readers have long heard the law and the prophets in those two figures' is a common reading, offered as a reading, not as the text.
Practice invites the Beatitude line 'blessed are the peacemakers' (paraphrased, not quoted).

Editor pass: cut 'for months' and 'the text says they see him truly' (not in Matthew 17), softened 'readers have long heard' to 'some readers hear', removed the superlative 'the gentlest moment', and replaced 'Orthodox Christians treasure this feast' with a plain statement that Orthodox churches keep it.

Audit pass (fresh auditor, 2026-10-01): replaced the unsourced character line 'Peter, who never could stay quiet' with Mark 9:6 (he did not know what to say); cut 'a light that heals' (nothing in the Transfiguration story heals) and a repeated 'afraid' line; the trapdoor scholar floor only restated the hook, so it now gives Luke 9:31 (they spoke of his 'decease', Greek exodos). Keeper: confirm exodos (ἔξοδον) in Luke 9:31.
